title: Component codes: resistors, capacitors, polarity and fuses
summary: How to read the values printed or painted on resistors, capacitors and fuses, and which way round polarised parts go. Use it before you trust or reuse a salvaged part.

steps.text: Clean the part and read it under a bright light with a magnifier. Burnt or faded bands are common: measure the resistor out of circuit instead.
Check a capacitor’s voltage rating is above anything you will put across it, and that the can isn’t bulging or crusty.
Check polarity before soldering a part in: reversed electrolytic and tantalum capacitors can burst.
Replace a fuse only with one of the same current and speed, and a voltage rating at least as high.
steps.warn: Never fit a bigger fuse, a wire or foil: the fuse is what stops a fault becoming a fire.

notes:
## Resistor colour bands

Hold the resistor with the bands bunched at the left; the tolerance band (often gold or silver) is on the right, sometimes after a gap. Four bands: digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Five bands: three digits, multiplier, tolerance.

| Colour | Digit | Multiplier | Tolerance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Black | 0 | ×1 | |
| Brown | 1 | ×10 | ±1% |
| Red | 2 | ×100 | ±2% |
| Orange | 3 | ×1 k | |
| Yellow | 4 | ×10 k | |
| Green | 5 | ×100 k | ±0.5% |
| Blue | 6 | ×1 M | ±0.25% |
| Violet | 7 | ×10 M | ±0.1% |
| Grey | 8 | ×100 M | ±0.05% (newer parts ±0.01%) |
| White | 9 | ×1 G | |
| Gold | | ×0.1 | ±5% |
| Silver | | ×0.01 | ±10% |

Examples: brown, black, red, gold is 1, 0 and ×100: 1 kΩ ±5%. Yellow, violet, orange is 47 kΩ.

## Surface-mount resistor codes

- **Three digits**: two digits, then the number of zeros. 103 is 10 kΩ, 472 is 4.7 kΩ.
- **Four digits** (1% parts): three digits, then the number of zeros. 1002 is 10 kΩ.
- **R marks the decimal point**: 4R7 is 4.7 Ω, R10 is 0.1 Ω (a current-sense resistor).
- **Two digits and a letter** (EIA-96, such as 01C): look it up in an EIA-96 table; 01C is 10 kΩ.
- **0 or 000** is a zero-ohm link: just a jumper.

## Capacitor codes

- Electrolytic cans and big film capacitors print the value and voltage: 470 µF 25 V.
- Small ceramic and film capacitors use three digits in picofarads, the third being the number of zeros: 104 is 100,000 pF (100 nF or 0.1 µF), 103 is 10 nF, 222 is 2.2 nF, 470 is 47 pF.
- A letter after the digits is the tolerance: J ±5%, K ±10%, M ±20%, Z +80/−20%.
- A digit-and-letter code is the voltage: 1H 50 V, 2A 100 V, 2E 250 V, 2G 400 V, 2J 630 V.
- **X2 and Y2** mark mains safety capacitors. Keep them for mains jobs, and never replace one with an ordinary capacitor.

## Which way round

| Part | Marking |
|---|---|
| Electrolytic capacitor | The stripe with − signs is negative; the longer leg is positive |
| Tantalum capacitor | The stripe or bar is **positive**: the opposite of an electrolytic |
| Diode | The band is the cathode (−) end; current flows towards the band |
| LED | The longer leg is +; the flat edge on the rim is − |
| Chip | Pin 1 is next to the dot or notch; pins count anticlockwise seen from above |

## Fuses

- **Sizes**: 5 × 20 mm glass in electronics; 6.3 × 32 mm (¼ × 1¼ in) in older equipment and appliances; blade fuses in vehicles.
- **Markings**: F is fast, T is time-delay (slow-blow, for motors and transformers); then the current; L or H is low or high breaking capacity (ceramic bodies are usually H); then the voltage. T3.15AH250V is slow-blow, 3.15 A, high breaking capacity, 250 V.
- **Thermal fuses** in kettles, heaters, hair dryers and motors are small cans or tubes marked with a temperature (such as 152 °C). They don't reset.

Standard, mini and low-profile blade fuses (maxi fuses use other colours):

| Blade fuse colour | Amps |
|---|---|
| Violet | 3 |
| Tan | 5 |
| Brown | 7.5 |
| Red | 10 |
| Blue | 15 |
| Yellow | 20 |
| Clear | 25 |
| Green | 30 |
| Orange | 40 |
